title: SECTION III — DEW, THRESHOLD AND THE AFFECTION OF HOME
summary: A quieter sequence centred on home, threshold, courtyard, child, speech, earth and belonging. The poems repeatedly approach the familiar from a slight distance—through mist, cloud, an open door, another person’s gaze or the stillness inside the self—so that affection becomes a way of seeing rather than merely possessing.

entries.title: Beyond the Threshold
entries.summary: A meditation on earth & natural imagery, dream & wakefulness and home & belonging. It moves from earth & natural imagery toward home & belonging, allowing the poem’s emphasis to change as it develops. Close reading (PDF p. 217; printed p. 216): The dew and the speaker’s feet place perception inside an already existing world. Looking makes the world present to the speaker, but does not bring that world into existence. The threshold thus marks a limit to the self’s authority as well as an entrance into familiar ground. Affection for home can coexist with this restraint: belonging does not require the claim that everything depends on one’s own gaze.

entries.title: Affection at an Unknown Ghat
entries.summary: A meditation on earth & natural imagery, language & meaning and body & consciousness. The recurring register of river and shore imagery helps carry the poem’s movement. Close reading (PDF p. 218; printed p. 217): A letter from a distant ghat raises the difference between receiving testimony and encountering a place through touch or sight. The misreading of a moonlit reflection does not make the water unreal; the error belongs to a particular judgement. This careful distinction also governs expectation. A hope about what comes next is not a guarantee. The poem lets affection inhabit uncertainty without converting desire into evidence.

entries.title: The Bird of Speech
entries.summary: A meditation on language & meaning, home & belonging and body & consciousness. It moves from home & belonging toward language & meaning, allowing the poem’s emphasis to change as it develops. Close reading (PDF p. 219; printed p. 218): A child’s drawing of a boat gives form to a journey that has not taken place. Speech is equally capable of doing more than reporting an existing fact: the force of an ordinary word changes with the situation in which it is spoken. A call, request and warning demand different responses. The poem’s domestic setting makes this account of meaning practical, while unspoken affection extends communication beyond the words themselves.

entries.title: Footprints of the Cloud
entries.summary: A meditation on earth & natural imagery, work & material life and body & consciousness. It moves from earth & natural imagery toward body & consciousness, allowing the poem’s emphasis to change as it develops. Close reading (PDF p. 220; printed p. 219): Wet traces permit an inference, but they do not justify every hope about the sky. The poem asks the reader to keep evidence and expectation distinct. It then makes room for other kinds of language: delight in beauty and the demand to save a bird do not function like weather reports. Their significance depends on appreciation and action. Different utterances can matter deeply without making the same kind of claim.
